utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar - good morning to everyone - could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we resume, there is a matter I would briefly like to deal with in private session, so we go into private session for only a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Ivetic, you'll understand that if possible the Chamber would appreciate if it would be -- if you could conclude your cross-examination today and preferably even leaving some time for additional questions by the Prosecution or by the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'll try to do so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Nicolai.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic will now continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, General. And I'll begin with my questions right away to try and be as efficient as possible. I'd like to first talk about something that was contained in a proofing information report which we received from the Office of the Prosecutor that indicates: "The witness confirmed that he had relatively regular contact with General Mladic from the beginning of his deployment in February 1995 through the fall of the Srebrenica enclave with the departure of the Dutch Battalion in July 1995. The witness stated that his contact with General Mladic was mostly by telephone and occasionally in writing." First of all, sir, is this information that I've been provided and which I've now read back to you true and correct?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ninety per cent of my contacts with the headquarters of BSA were with my counterpart, Chief of Staff, Milovanovic. Incidentally, I would get other persons on the phone, including General Mladic at times.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with that clarification, now, is the rest of what I read accurate and truthful?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I also wrote letters on a number of occasions and they in all cases addressed General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me break it down. On occasions when you had telephonic contact with General Mladic, would those have almost always have been with the same Croatian translator Svetlana that we talked about yesterday?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I stated before, in almost all cases, this was Svetlana the Croatian interpreter. On occasion, if unexpectedly something would happen and Svetlana was not present, I would use one of the military interpreters that were present there at the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. And now I want to talk about the written letters that were sent to General Mladic. Did you always send a Serbo-Croatian translation of the letter and, if so, who was responsible for translating the document into Serbo-Croat?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Translations were always sent along and they would be made by one of the interpreters, those translations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the proofing information report from the Prosecution also indicates that one of the topics which you discussed with General Mladic was in relation to VRS complaints about Armija BiH attacks on Serb territory originating from within the Srebrenica enclave; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then I would like to spend a few moments talking about this before we return to some more general items. Do you recall, sir, how many times or at least how frequently the VRS was complaining to UNPROFOR about the Armija BiH undertaking attacks originating from within the Srebrenica enclave and attacking Serb territory?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't be really sure. I wasn't keeping track of that, but if I were to make an estimate, I would think about five times in the period that I was Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, on these occasions, did you receive such complaints directly or were they forwarded to you by DutchBat or some other UNPROFOR unit?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a number of cases, I received them direct. However, I can't rule out that incidentally we would receive a warning indirectly through DutchBat and the headquarters and from there to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did you also receive complaints from the VRS about the Armija BiH forces conducting military attacks originating from within Bihac or any of the other UN protected areas attacking Serb territories surrounding those protected areas?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. I actually think that that is what this discussion is about, so I'd have to say yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to focus for the time being on the safe area of Srebrenica. First of all, if we can return to your Rule 92 ter statement, which is P1165 marked for identification, and if we could turn to paragraph 8 which is at the top of page 3 in the English and also in the B/C/S. Here you state that during a meeting with Mr. Silajdzic of the Bosnian Muslim side, you reminded him that you could use air support, you being UNPROFOR, against the Muslim side if they used their weapons in breach of Security Council Resolutions 824, 836 and 844. And I want to ask you, sir, did you or anyone else at BH command ever threaten to use air support against the Armija of BiH in Srebrenica for these attacks that took place from within the enclave of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I very clearly remember this one instance and it was I who made that actual comment. It might be because there was a meeting later on with representatives of BiH that this was repeated, but I dare not say with certainty, but no more often than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just so that we are clear, this meeting that's discussed in paragraph 9 with Mr. Silajdzic, that occurred sometime early in May of 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And how about Bihac? Did you or anyone else at BH command of UNPROFOR ever threaten to use close air support against the Bosnian Muslim side under these same UN Security Council resolutions as to attacks they conducted from within the Bihac enclave attacking Serb territories surrounding the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you refer to paragraph 9, but I thought it was in the same discussion with Silajdzic and that is in 8, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours, it is 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, in relation to Bihac, did you or anyone else at BH Command ever threaten the use of air support against the Bosnian Muslim side under these same UN Security Council resolutions relating to attacks which they conducted from within the Bihac enclave?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can't recall that. And actually I deem it very unlikely because deploying air attacks against military that exfiltrate and often during the night would conduct attacks on villages outside an enclave, it would be very hard to use a weapon against that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. At that time, what was your understanding and was it the similar understanding of the BH command as to these three Security Council resolutions? Did they apply equally to the Armija BiH violations as well as to the VRS violations?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And was there a consensus of what was to be considered a violation and what was not a violation, again at the level of the BH command?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the Security Council resolutions, it states very clearly that air attacks can be used for attacks on positions of UN military as well as in situations where the civilian population is being attacked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I take it that your previous questions about equally being applied requires a bit more of an analysis of what is exactly found in the resolutions, but if your question was: Where armed forces are addressed or governments are addressed in those resolutions without further specification, that it would apply to both parties? Is that what you intended to ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is that how you understood that question, Mr. Nicolai?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is how I understood the question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you are aware that the Chamber is very -- wants to be very precise in analysing these international texts, what obligations are found in it and what tasks are given in it, et cetera. But for the time being we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General, I'd like to focus with you on Srebrenica. Was it your understanding from these resolutions along with other documents and agreements from the time period in 1993 that the enclave of Srebrenica was supposed to be demilitarised such that no combatants were supposed to be left armed in the enclave itself?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that that was the idea, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did such a regime apply to the other safe area enclaves such as Zepa, Gorazde, Bihac and Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Definitely. And it's also true that for all those enclaves, the heavy arms which are also most easily identified were stored at so-called weapon collection points, and these were also under the control of the UN. However, it is evident that it be much harder with individuals that have very light hand arms to track them down because those weapons are so much easier to hide.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, let's digress from Srebrenica into Sarajevo, sir. Were any efforts actually made by BH command to enforce the demilitarisation as to infantry weapons in Sarajevo where the weapons were not so difficult to find?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When military were found or Muslim fighters were found with weapons and they would be disarmed but it's an illusion to suppose that in a city you would not be able to hide any hand arms, so that there be a situation where you could disarm everybody is truly a mission impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But, sir, were the Muslim fighters in Sarajevo really hiding their weapons from UNPROFOR, their infantry weapons?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not always. And there were times that there were fierce fighting at the borders of the enclave between Muslim fighters and the Serb fighters with heavy firing of hand arms. However, these are moments at which it's not very easy to start disarming either one of the parties, and I'm sure that's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is. I'd like to look at some documents with you. And the first I would like to look at is 65 ter number 17956, and I would like the first page in e-court so we can look at it together. And I can tell you that this is an April 18 1993 agreement signed by Generals Halilovic, Mladic and General Wahlgren of the UNPROFOR, and I would like to look at - once it comes up - paragraph 4 of the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While waiting for it, Mr. Ivetic, exactly that happened what I was concerned about, that is that you put the demilitarisation in Sarajevo at exactly the same footing as any of the others, whereas we've seen many instruments which make a distinction between the two. But I'll let you go, but that's what I tried to avoid and that's what nevertheless happened. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, first of all, let me direct you to the part that I would like to read from paragraph number 4 for you and ask you about it: "All weapons, ammunition, mines, explosives and combat supplies except medicines inside Srebrenica will be submitted, handed over, to UNPROFOR under the supervision of three officers from each side who -- with control carried out by UNPROFOR. No armed persons or units except UNPROFOR will remain within the city once the demilitarisation process is complete. Responsibility for the demilitarisation process remains with UNPROFOR." Sir, I want to ask you, at the time that you were deployed to be Chief of Staff at BH command in Sarajevo, was this document or the requirements of this provision one of the things that you were briefed on and made aware of when assuming your position?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document as such, I never had before me. But the fact that in the enclaves, and in this case specifically in Srebrenica, the fighters had to be demilitarised, that was something I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now I'd like to look at I believe it's Exhibit P00023 in e-court. And this is again an agreement relating to Srebrenica signed by General Halilovic, General Mladic and General Morillon this time of UNPROFOR dated 8 May 1993. And, again, if we could have the first page, sir, if you could take a moment to look at the title of this page in the English version that is before us, do you believe that such a document was of the type that you were made aware of upon your deployment to Sarajevo in February of 1995?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first have to read it. I've read it and the document itself, I don't know. The content, however, has more or less the same purport as the earlier quote that you read to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to ask you about specific parts of it, see if that comports with what you understood the regime to be in Srebrenica. First I'd like to look at Article 2, which is at the bottom of the first page in English and it's at pages 2 to 3 of the B/C/S version in e-court. And, sir, if you could follow along with me from the English, it says as follows: "On the ground, the demilitarised zone shall be marked by UNPROFOR by means of boards on which is stated in English, Serbian and Bosnian, written in Cyrillic and Latin as follows: Demilitarised zone, any military operation is strictly forbidden. Article 60 Protocol I additional to the Geneva Conventions." Sir, does this comport with your understanding and recollection of the safe area regime that was supposed to be in effect in Srebrenica during the time that you were Chief of Staff to General Smith at the BH command?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement about the boards that were supposed to be -- to be placed there is not something I know about and I don't know to what extent this actually happened. But the fact that this -- these were the agreements that there would be no military operations inside those borders. Those demarcations, well, naturally I know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'd like to ask you was it your recollection that the definition of a demilitarised zone was according to -- was supposed to be according to Article 60 of Protocol I of the additions to the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Honestly, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to now turn to page 2 in the English and page 3 in the B/C/S to briefly look at Article 3 to again see if this provision is consistent with the knowledge and understanding that you had of the regime when you were Chief of Staff to General Smith in 1995: "Every military or paramilitary unit will have either to withdraw from the demilitarised zone or submit, hand over their weapons, ammunition, mines, explosives and combat supplies in the demilitarised zone will be handed over, submitted to UNPROFOR." Sir, is this provision something consistent with your understanding of what the safe area regime was supposed to be in Srebrenica in 1995?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Entirely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down this page to Article 5 of the same in both languages, and, sir, again I'd like to ask you to follow along as I read, and my question will again be the same, if it's consistent with your understanding of the regime that was in place: "UNPROFOR shall control the demilitarised zone. To be able to implement this, an UNPROFOR unit and UNMOs with sufficient strength to control the area shall be present in the demilitarised zone. Until the contracting parties agree otherwise, the UNPROFOR strength shall be of at least a company group with command and supplying elements in each demilitarised zone. In order to be able to resupply, and rotate the unit, UNPROFOR shall have freedom of movement to and from the demilitarised zone. Non-combatants who are in or who are willing to enter the demilitarised zone except members of UNPROFOR are not permitted to have in their possession any weapon, ammunition, or explosives. Weapons, ammunition and explosives in their possession shall be seized by UNPROFOR. Combatants will not be allowed to enter or to be in the demilitarised zone." Is this provision consistent with your knowledge and understanding of the safe area regime that was supposed to be in place in Srebrenica in 1995 when you were Chief of Staff to General Smith?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It definitely comports with that. And I'd like to add right away that all those provisions, also the first one listed here about free access from and to the enclave, that against all those provisions there were violations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you, sir, would you agree with me that the safe area of Srebrenica enclave that in fact was never demilitarised such that the Armija BiH forces within the enclave remained armed and active in 1995 all the way up until the fall of Srebrenica in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't quite agree with you. Where you say they were never completely demilitarised I must say you're right. However, there were considerable quantities of weapons seized. I saw the weapon collection point with my own eyes and there was quite a store there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And the weapons collection point was primarily or was entirely heavy weapons; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mainly. But also a considerable quantity of hand weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you, as Chief of Staff of BH command in 1995, understand that the demilitarisation of UN declared safe areas, including Srebrenica, extended to infantry or small arms in addition to heavy weapons?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was informed about that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to confront you with something that General Rupert Smith testified about at transcript page 7524, line 20, to 7543, line 2, at this trial at which time he testified that he didn't think that the exclusion zone and agreements, demilitarisation agreements did not cover small arms. Was he right about that or are you right that infantry and small arms were part of the demilitarisation agreements as to the safe areas?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in as far as I know, this also applied to small arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, what information or knowledge did the BH command of UNPROFOR have at that time when you were Chief of Staff to General Smith as to the number of armed -- excuse me, of Armija BiH fighters that were still present in the enclave of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, we were given regular information about that, and I think it must have been from 2.000 to 3.000 BiH military that were in the enclave. To what extent they were still all armed at that time, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And how about in the enclaves of Gorazde, Bihac and Zepa? Did you have any information as to the amount of BiH fighters that were still present in those safe areas?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That information was absolutely available. However, I can't recall it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fair enough, sir. I'd like to -- I'd like to go through something which you testified about in the Tolimir trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for that purpose, I'd like to call up 65 ter 1D931 which is a transcript from the 17th of August, 2010, and the e-court page is 18 at the bottom, continuing on to page 19, and that comports to transcript page 3990 through 3991.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could look at line 21 - I apologise - and if you could follow along with me, sir, I'd have a question after I read this section: "Q. Then, please, General, tell us whether you had reports about the activities of the Muslim forces from the protected areas of Srebrenica and Zepa which they conducted immediately prior to the operation that took place in Zepa and Srebrenica? And we are talking about the month of June and July. Thank you. So did your command have that? Thank you. "A. When Muslim troops tried to carry out actions outside the limits of the enclave, and it was observed by UNPROFOR, then of course it would be reported. Now, we did receive some incidental reports about that but except for noting that they had, we couldn't do anything besides note that they had crossed the borders of the enclave because we had no means to observe outside the limits of the enclave because we were denied access to the Serb territory. So we couldn't see what they were doing there. And as I've stated at previous hearings, the means and opportunities for UNPROFOR units to observe properly were greatly complicated by, first, the lack of fuel which made it impossible to carry out motorised patrols, and because some of the UNPROFOR soldiers were blocked by Serb troops and unable to return from leave which had seriously compromised the numbers of our troops and they were no longer able to perform their duties properly. So the number of observations was therefore undoubtedly more limited than what was actually happening." Now, sir, first I have to ask you: Do you stand by this testimony that you gave in this other case as being both truthful and accurate as to the section that I have just gone through with you?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think this is a fine reflection.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to ask you about specific portions of it. First of all, when you say that the -- you had no way of -- you were denied access and couldn't see what was going on there, am I correct that BH command had at its disposal the resources of NATO and the NATO overflights in particular, both manned and unmanned flights, with the capability of -- with a camera recording what was happening in a particular village or what a particular village looked like? Am I correct that you had that ability?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UN as such did not have these means or resources but it could ask NATO to do exploratory flights or use drones to survey specific areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did BH command ever ask NATO to do so?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Undoubtedly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you told us that the G-2 at BH command had a direct link to the HQ in Naples of NATO and had access to satellite and other surveillance. Was that utilised in relation to the complaints of Muslim forces burning villages surrounding Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in relation with these specific complaints I do not know. Moreover, at a time that such a complaint comes in, the fact has usually already taken place. So the only thing that one might be able to observe in retrospect is whether there was any destruction inflicted and then it's always very much the question when and by whom that was inflicted. So in retrospect it is very hard to ascertain that with those specific means.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'd like to focus on the parts of this answer that dealt with the inability to carry out duties because of the forces that were not permitted to return from leave. We had a member of the DutchBat testifying here last week, Mr. van Duijn, who at transcript page 10341, lines 1 through 8, testified that as to the DutchBat deployment, even before Dutch troops went on leave, there still was not a sufficient amount of forces sent to the enclave to demilitarise an area the size of Srebrenica. Is it your contention that the original deployment size was sufficient to perform duties to demilitarise the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am absolutely convinced that from the start, there was absolutely insufficient troops present in the enclave to be able to do that task adequately. I think that instead of some 600, we would have needed around 6.000 to perform those tasks adequately.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And now I want to ask you about the part of your prior answer where you talked about not being able to see what the Muslim forces were doing on Serb territory. I'd like to present you with something that Mr. van Duijn testified about at transcript page 10346 through 10347 answering Judge Orie. And I think I will read it out for you in full so that you have the benefit of that when listening to my question. It begins at line 12 and goes through line 2 of the next page: "Judge Orie: Mr. Ivetic, I'm a bit puzzled by one of the previous answers. The question was whether you ever found out about or hear stories about Muslim soldiers going out from the Srebrenica enclave burning down Serb villages. Your answer was, 'I've heard stories about that, yes, in other areas that were not under my responsibility but in the enclave.' Did you want to say that you heard it in the enclave or that it happened in the enclave because the question was about going out of the enclave. "The witness: It did not happen in the enclave. I heard it from other commanders, colleagues of mine from DutchBat, that were responsible for other areas and that had seen from their observation posts or patrols or from Muslim commanders in the area that they would leave the enclave and enter the Serb area and then burn down villages. "Judge Orie: Yes, thank you." Now, sir, the question I have for you is: Do you recall if you had reports from DutchBat commanders that they could see from their own observation posts and also heard from the Muslim commanders that the Muslims were leaving the enclave and burning down Serb villages?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I remember concretely is that there were notifications that it was observed from the OPs that Muslim combatants would leave the enclave, but from those OPs they were not able to see what subsequently happened or was done by those combatants in that territory, on Serb territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay, sir. I'd like to look at Exhibit P1182 which was a document that the Prosecution used with you yesterday. If we could have that up in e-court. And if you recall, this was a letter that you wrote to General Mladic on the 26th of June, 1995. And I'd like to ask you about the first paragraph which reads as follows: "In response to your letter number 06/17-441 of 24 June 1995, with reports on several attacks from the safe area of Srebrenica, I ordered an immediate investigation. That investigation made me recognise that at the times and places mentioned in your letter, combat activities by BiH troops had really occurred." Now, I want to ask you, after conducting an investigation and after confirming that the complaints made by General Mladic were confirmed by facts, what did BH command do in relation to the BiH Muslims?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, your question is more or less twofold. The investigation that was conducted was unable to confirm this, simply for the reason that those observations were not there, that events had in fact taken place as had been alleged by General Mladic. Nevertheless, we did get in touch with the BiH command, we informed them about these complaints, and gave them severe warning that were they to conduct such activity, this would be deemed provocation for BSA with possible consequences in the shape of acts against the population in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, correct me if I'm wrong, but you were able to confirm that combat operations were conducted by the BiH. Was that not a violation of the Srebrenica safe area regime that no military operations were to be conducted?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, obviously, it was part of the agreement that those troops could most definitely not go outside the enclave. However, we were not able to prevent this in each and every case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you, in your previous answer to my question you said that you complained to the BiH command, the Bosnian Muslim command, that these would be considered provocations. Isn't it correct that you never complained to them about these being actual violations of the accords that were in place as to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, but I did, with some regularity, this was a point of discussion on all levels, both Colonel Karremans spoke to the representatives present in Srebrenica, but also on other levels we repeatedly insisted that it was absolutely necessary for all parties to comply with the agreements that had been made.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was there a consensus under -- within the BH command originating from General Smith, that military air strikes against the Bosnian Muslims were off the table?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard somebody say that this was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'd now like to ask you about something slightly different in relation to demilitarisation of Srebrenica. Mr. van Duijn last week also testified about what happened when Observation Post Echo fell in 1995; that is transcript page 10348 through 10349. First of all, sir, do you recall during your tenure that there was a time period when one of the observation posts, Echo, was taken over?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall a time period during your tenure as Chief of Staff when one of the observation posts in Srebrenica code named E, or Echo, fell, was taken over?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe if we can correct the record -- oh, thank you, it has now been corrected.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And by whom was that observation post allegedly taken over?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: By the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't really recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, sir. Without being able to fix the date of that, I do want to ask you about what Mr. van Duijn testified about at 10349, transcript lines 13 through 17. At that time he said that he received a communication from his DutchBat superiors which he viewed as a directive to turn a "blind eye" to the Bosnian Muslims' weapons in Srebrenica. Did BH command of UNPROFOR know of any such directive having been given to DutchBat personnel within the enclave of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I know nothing about that, and it sounds absolutely absurd.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you believe that such a directive would have been consistent with the obligations of UNPROFOR and the mission, as you understood it, as to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Of course, it is absolutely opposed to the actual task we were there to fulfil. I would understand if a patrol on foot, five men, would get to a platoon, 40 men that were also armed, that they would not be able to demilitarise that group of 40. However, the least they could do is report the fact that this incident took place, where the incident took place, et cetera, and why no action was taken. But looking the other way intentionally is something I can't imagine took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm sorry, I switched channels by mistake. I think it would be helpful if Mr. Ivetic read the quote that he read to Lieutenant-Colonel van Duijn which I think would put this matter in perspective and in context in framing the question to General Nicolai, and that can be found at the page that Mr. Ivetic referred to except he didn't read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I believe that I accurately --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's not debate. Isn't it true, but help me if I'm wrong in my recollection, that this happened according to that witness in the days immediately preceding the moving in of the Bosnian Serb troops?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct, after Operation Post Echo fell which is what I asked him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but -- but you said you can't give an exact time. I don't know whether it was clear from your question to the witness that the testimony was about that point in time. So when he says it's absurd, it may be that the timing is relevant for the judgement you asked him as a matter of fact to give. You were not asking for facts but you were asking for judgement. Perhaps you could make that part of the context for which you asked that judgement of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm confused because my question very specifically dealt with the fall of Observation Post Echo and at that time that this was said to Commander van Duijn, so how much clearer can I be?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I think the witness said he didn't know when that happened, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore he's totally lost as far as time is concerned, he has more than six months available. The fall of Observation Post Echo was, I think it was around 8 July, it was then that happened what Mr. van Duijn said happened. Would that cause your answer to be the same or would that change anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. That doesn't change anything of my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, I take it that this was the context you were seeking, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It is, Mr. President, but there was a specific quote that Mr. Ivetic read to Lieutenant van Duijn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there is anything specific in that quote you can do that in re-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One other thing Mr. van Duijn testified about was situations when he witnessed what he believed to be helicopter flights into Srebrenica and DutchBat patrols finding remnants of US military emergency rations at the same time when Serbs claim that the Americans were arming the Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica. And he testified at transcript page 10350 that his requests for AWACS support to identify if there were any such flights was not able to be completed because coincidentally the AWACS were said to be not available. Did you obtain reports of such things from the Dutch Battalion in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is the question "do you" or "did you"?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: All that is asserted here, I am reading now for the first time and I have never heard about this before.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Am I correct that at the time in 1995, that the Americans were operating the AWACS planes that were providing support to UNPROFOR and the NATO missions in Bosnia at that time?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was, and I would assume that this is known, an operation deny flight where NATO air fighters would try to prevent all other air flights above the territory, and that operation was ongoing also at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe we are at the point for the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are, Mr. Ivetic. Could the witness first be escorted out of the courtroom. We will take a break of 20 minutes, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take a break and resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Ivetic, the Chamber observed that major portions of the evidence you elicited before the break, at least that's the impression of the Chamber, are matters which are not very much in dispute, which are matters on which you have led already quite some evidence through other witnesses, and where at least the Chamber is not aware of major challenge to those matters, and as far as relevance is concerned, the Chamber asked itself whether this was the core of the case or whether this was background, and if it is background, and the Chamber tends to think that it is for major parts, then it should get the size of background and not replace what seems to be the core of the case. Could you please keep this in mind when you are using your time in the hours to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will, Your Honours and I do want to also bring to Your Honours' attention that a significant part of the questions that I asked dealt with matters that another witness testified about and so it goes towards the credibility of that testimony by the other witness who is superior to this witness within the command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That may explain 15 per cent of your time, not more. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you about a document, sir, Exhibit D140 and I'd like to call it up in e-court and look at the same with you. I think when the first page comes up we will see that it originated from within the BH command, and if we can turn to the next page of the document we will see it's an English rendition of a letter received by General Smith from General Mladic, and it states in the first section as follows: "Dear general, we are gravely concerned over the frequent use of Tuzla airport by the Muslim side. The aircrafts are bringing weapons, ammunition and war materials for their needs. Unfortunately this pirate activity of their aircraft is enabled by the NATO air force and the Muslim army does not allow your forces to control the loads. I am sure you share my opinion that these activities are seriously jeopardising the signed agreements and represent a serious breach of the truce and of relevant Security Council resolutions. I ask you to take urgent measures to stop these peace-threatening activities, otherwise we will be compelled to take the necessary measures regarding the Muslim side's violations of the Tuzla safe area which is in the presence of your forces turning into a war base for Islamic countries." Now, given the date of this letter being just before your deployment, were you briefed about such complaints pertaining to the use of the Tuzla air base at the time of your arrival as Chief of Staff to BH command?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To start, let me point out to you that this letter dates from before my arrival or the commencement of my position as Chief of Staff at UNPROFOR, it dates to 13 February, and I did not arrive until late February in Sarajevo. However, I did indeed hear that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I invite you to carefully listen to the question because the question started with "date of this letter being just before your deployment," so that was already part of the question. But please proceed with your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. I did indeed hear that allegedly there had been resupplies through the airport of Tuzla and I know that investigations were started and everything was done to prevent that that sort of things would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to move to a second document, D142 an exhibit in e-court, and it is again a communication from General Mladic complaining to General Smith of an incident a little closer in time to your deployment, I believe on the 23rd of February, and I'll direct your attention to the part that reads as follows: "On 23 February 1995, at about 2010 hours, a transport plane with weapons and military equipment landed again at Tuzla airport's secondary runway. It was escorted by two NATO fighter aircraft which were protecting it during flight and offloading. Unfortunately, this has been repeated lately in front within sight and hearing of NATO and UNPROFOR forces, both in the air and at Tuzla airport itself. These forces are doing nothing to prevent the violations of the relevant UN Security Council resolutions prohibiting the import of weapons and military equipment." Now, again, were you briefed of this specific type of incident where it is alleged that NATO aircraft provided escort or support to flights bringing military weapons to the Bosnian Muslim side in late February 1995, albeit again a few days before your deployment?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that this had allegedly happened, and I repeat what I just said. UNPROFOR took measures to prevent that this would be repeated, and as far as I know, during my period there it never did happen again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What did you, as the person with command over the G-2 intelligence officer Lieutenant-Colonel Powers within BH command do vis-a-vis your ability to contact NATO to confirm or deny whether in fact NATO aircraft had participated in such an arming campaign?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly what happened there because it did take place before I came onboard, but I take it that at the highest level the authorities of UNPROFOR and NATO got in touch so as to insist that this sort of activity would be ceased, and at the airport of Tuzla, was also the headquarters of the north-east sectors, and so I think it was within our possibilities to actually have control over this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: To your knowledge, either directly or indirectly, did anyone at BH command ever attempt to get confirmation from NATO of whether NATO had been involved or NATO aircraft or aircraft of NATO member nations had been involved in this arming these convoys, these air convoys, into Tuzla airport?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I recall, as far as that is concerned, is that indeed it was seen that aircraft landed there, their nationality was not ascertained at that time. But I cannot but conclude, in view of the control that NATO had over the air territory, that that would have happened at least with the permission or consent of NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now I'd like to return and focus with you on the 6th of July, 1995, in Srebrenica. And I think at your 92 ter statement which is P1165 marked for identification, we need to look at page 9 in both languages, at paragraph number 41, where you're talking about this day. And you talk first about of how around the 6th of July in the morning there was heavy fighting between the VRS and the ABiH. You say that the VRS were using between five to ten tanks and heavy artillery, the shelling was mostly directed at military targets and not directly against the civilian population. And that day -- you say: "That day I talked with the commander of DutchBat about using air power, I explained to him that day of the policies of General Janvier and Smith. I said that according to the actual guidelines the use of air power was permitted for the self-defence of UNPROFOR soldiers or in case of deliberate attacks on the civilian population." I want to ask you, sir, first of all, during this time period, 6th of July, am I to understand that the Armija BiH from within Srebrenica enclave was firing or was exchanging fire with the Serb forces located around Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't exactly recall but, yes, yes, it says it here in the report that there was fierce fighting between the army and the ABH so that must have been the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now, looking at paragraph 42 of your statement, which is on the next page in both languages, it is recorded that the 7th of July, Friday, was a rather quiet day, probably because of the bad weather conditions. I want to ask you: Did this assessment relate to both the activities of the VRS and the Armija BiH in Srebrenica and around Srebrenica on that day?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. I just know that it was a relatively quiet day, which is not to say that nothing happened. However, in comparison with the day before, confrontations were less fierce.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to the 8th of July, which is also detailed in your statement, would it be fair to summarise it that again, both sides were still militarily active and fighting?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I want to focus on paragraph 45 of your statement, in the middle part of the same, which is on this same page that we have here and it's the part that starts with: "Zagreb made it clear that General Janvier did not want to use this ultimate solution without DutchBat having first used their weapons. He wanted a step to be taken before the calling in of air attacks. According to the results of these consultations, we gave orders to DutchBat to take blocking positions south of Srebrenica town so that if the VRS attacked the town this would not only be an attack on the civilian population but also an attack on UNPROFOR troops. In this case all the conditions for using air power would be met. This order was carried out by DutchBat?" I want to ask you, sir, am I correctly interpreting this that the order for DutchBat to take blocking positions in Srebrenica was in essence to create the pretext for the ability to call in close air support against the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct, and formally it was not absolutely necessary based on the council Resolution A 24 and 36 because they offered ample opportunity already to be able to use air space. However, because of the additional restrictions imposed from the headquarters in Zagreb concerning the use of air support, General Janvier explicitly wanted that first the UNPROFOR troops would react with other means to the attack of the BSA before he was willing to deploy the air arms, the air weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From the answer, which by the way I listened to in English, it's unclear to me whether the witness has well understood your question. It being a pretext that it is that they were seeking a reason to start air strikes but that the blocking positions were ordered in order to create such a situation. Was that the case? Or was it, and that seems to be your explanation, that only in last resort, until other means had been used, that only in last resort Zagreb was willing to order air strikes. Which of the two is it? Or any third explanation is of course welcome as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, given the fact that the quantity of troops still available to halt any attack from the BSA was absolutely insufficient, this order was very consciously given so as to create a situation in which there would be both an attack on UNPROFOR and on the city of Srebrenica. And in that case, there was no doubt whatsoever about the legitimacy of the deployment of air strikes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That seems to be a third explanation, that the blocking positions were ordered in order to provoke more or less an attack on the town, which then would justify air strikes. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, not to provoke the attack. It was intended to draw a clear line in the sand up to this point, but no further. Then if you come further we will deploy air strikes. And so obviously BSA had the choice to withdraw its troops then and to say, Okay, if that is your position, we will go, we'll halt our attacks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, these blocking positions that were ordered on the 9th of July, am I correct that Armija BiH forces, armed Armija BiH forces, were deployed alongside the DutchBat APCs and fired upon the Serb troops that were approaching?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were not deployed by UNPROFOR. It is true that they were in position close to the blocking positions and whether they actually fired is not something I have any information on. You would have to ask the witnesses that were in Srebrenica at the time. However, they held positions close to the blocking positions, it is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What clear message did UNPROFOR, BH command, think that would send to the Serbs, deploying blocking positions at or near the places of deployment of Armija BiH forces?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no opinion on that. We had a very written -- clear written statement in which we said that UNPROFOR would take a position there and if it were to be attacked, that position, this would lead to deployment of air strikes. And what BiH would do at the same time is not something that we had any announcements about. We did not know in effect what they would do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, was actually your question: Wouldn't send this the message that UNPROFOR was siding with the forces? Why not directly ask it? I mean that's a clear issue, takes less time if you put it in one question. Mr. Ivetic wanted to know whether you do not think that this would send a message that UNPROFOR was siding with the Army of the BiH, and whether you would share such a view.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I absolutely do not share such a view. UNPROFOR had orders to protect the civilian population, and this is what they attempted to do from those blocking positions, and if the forces on the ground were not enough, then they would use forces in the air. There was absolutely no support to the Army of the BiH.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the question was whether by allowing the ABiH forces so close to the blocking positions, whether there was not a serious risk that it would be understood as siding. Mr. Ivetic, I take it that is what you were aiming at.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So irrespective of the intentions, what the effect might have been.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. That might possibly have been the case. However, it was hard enough to free up troops to take up those blocking positions and UNPROFOR absolutely did not avail of additional means to prevent that the BiH would take positions close to those blocking positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you, we've come to the 9th of July, and you've previously said that you did not know of any order to turn a blind eye to the Bosnian Muslim weapons at this time. I'd like to move to 10 July. Am I correct that by the 10th of July, BH command had made a decision and ordered DutchBat to make available to the Armija BiH the heavy weapons that were in the weapons collection point at one of the DutchBat company compounds?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. The BiH incidentally did not use them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you: What was the rationale or authority for permitting the BiH side to be offered to take back their heavy weapons from the weapons collection points in Srebrenica or was this again something that could amount to taking sides in a conflict, given the overall picture?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, this is putting the world on its head, isn't it? There was actually one party to wit the BSA who had for some days attempted to use every means they had to attack the enclave, including the Muslims that were inside it, and I don't think it's anything more than reasonable, and actually UNPROFOR I think waited long enough, where one party is violating agreements to such an extent that also the other party is given the means to resist this with all possible means.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then I have a question for you, sir, about the weapons collection points in Sarajevo where the Serbs had heavy weapons stored. Did they also have a right to take back those weapons to defend themselves in case of an attack by the BiH side that UNPROFOR was unable to stop under the regime and the agreements of the weapons exclusion zones that were in place, as you understood them, and in particular I'm talking about the time period of May 1995?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. I'm just reading the question again in the transcript in English. Yes. I think I understood the question. In May 1995, in Sarajevo, there was definitely not a matter of the use by heavy arms by BiH vis-a-vis the Serb forces, and also no cause, then, to give permission to the Serb forces to take their heavy arms that had been stored at those weapon collection points.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to now switch back to Srebrenica and 9th of July, 1995, and I want to take a look at P1152, which is the warning and press release that you discussed yesterday in direct examination, sent on 9 July to General Mladic and I guess to the world. And if we could have the second page of the same, and the text of this was shown to you yesterday and you confirmed having a role in generating this, and I think it is clear. Now I want to ask you about this because this document says that the Serbs resumed attacks on 7 July 1995. Will you agree with me, given your testimony today, that this press release and warning is factually not entirely correct as to the 7th of July, in that it was deemed a quiet day and thus the Serbs -- that the actions of the Serbs could not be described as they are described in this press release?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. That is a little curious, that after all those years you now point this out to me for the first time. It should have been 6th July to be exact, but I never noticed it before now that you indicate it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the document also claims that they fired indiscriminately into the safe area and directly targeted UN facilities causing several civilian deaths. Am I correct that the reference to several civilian deaths in this warning and press release is also not entirely correct?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I doubt very seriously because I know there were notifications that there were lethal casualties and we actually knew this because of the UNMOs' observations, among other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, do you recall who made the decision to include the not entirely correct allegation about the 7th of July, 1995, in this press release?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the entire text of this warning is the result of extensive telephone consultations between the headquarters in Sarajevo and the headquarters in Zagreb, and ultimately the responsibility for the text is with General Janvier or Mr. Akashi.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But it was sent to General Mladic and I take it it was a warning or, rather, a rationale for why air strikes might be considered against his forces, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And it was not sent to the Armija BiH side, which according to your prior testimony was engaged on the 6th of July, heavily fighting with the Serbs, exchanging fire with the Serbs, also a violation of the agreements; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But what we deemed much more serious was that the Serbs were attacking both the civilian population and the UNPROFOR forces, which was not the case with the activities of the BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I want to now move to the issue of the evacuation of refugees from the Srebrenica enclave, and I'd like to look at page 13 in English of your Rule 92 ter statement, P1165, and paragraph 59 of the same and it's also page 13 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, while waiting for the text to come on our screens, you were talking about violation of the agreements, plural. Which ones did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I had in mind the -- we have been talking with this witness about the regime of the safe areas as he understood it under the various Security Council resolutions and the various demilitarisation agreements which I went through with this witness and which he said he did not recall the actual documents. But the particular provision that I had read were ones that he was familiar with as applying to the overall regime in the safe area of Srebrenica. That's my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You were talking about agreements but you put two agreements to the witness, that those are the ones that you're talking about, okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At this paragraph, and I think we are talking about the 11th of July at this point in time, and I will read it for you it says: "Colonel Karremans commenced negotiations with General Mladic that night and I was advised for the first time that Mladic was on the ground there. The next day, the negotiations were to continue with Mladic. We were instructing Colonel Karremans on what he had to do during those negotiations -- these negotiations by telephone and in writing. We instructed him to stay with the civilian population so that he and his men could observe the evacuation in order that it would be carried out within the international rules. Directly after we stopped the air attacks we realised that the civilian population would have to be evacuated from Srebrenica. There was no food, enough medical care or even protection from the weather for the people there. We had hoped to do this under the cover of the UNPROFOR troops and even use UNPROFOR trucks if necessary. On the 11th of July, I had informed the Dutch minister of defence of the planned evacuation and our intention to use UNPROFOR trucks, and he had agreed to this." Now, just so that we are clear here, I want to make sure that I'm clear in understanding this as meaning that UNPROFOR BH command had instructed and ordered Colonel Karremans to negotiate with General Mladic to permit the evacuation of refugees from Srebrenica as early as 11 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. That would have been absolutely impossible because as you may recall, the end of the deployment of the air force was later that afternoon, and not until then was there contact between Mladic and Colonel Karremans and were there negotiations started about the conditions for evacuation. And I think, if I recall clearly, it was around 6.00 at the end of the afternoon, I was in touch with the Ministry of Defence in the Netherlands, and told the minister that we intended such an evacuation, but it may be clear that it takes some time to organise something like that. It's not simple. You have to get means of transport from somewhere to start an evacuation. And definitely we wouldn't have been able to do this on the same day. In the most favourable case we would have succeeded to do this on the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, then I ask for you to explain to me the section that says: "Directly after we stopped the air attacks, we realised that the civilian population would have to be evacuated from Srebrenica." Is this not "we," referring to UNPROFOR, making a decision that the evacuation of refugees from Srebrenica was a necessity before there was any contact with General Mladic on the ground?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We didn't need General Mladic's advice to be able to conclude that the situation of the refugees in those circumstances was an untenable one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And thus I suppose, sir, that the instructions and orders you sent to Colonel Karremans before he met with General Mladic for the first time would have dealt with the evacuation and the need for the refugees to be evacuated, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was -- I no longer needed to explain the necessity of this to Colonel Karremans. He could readily understand this, and it was also simply an order from UNPROFOR to Colonel Karremans that the evacuation would have to take place. However, naturally, we did have to inform him as to how we supposed this might take place before -- because for the execution we needed the co-operation of the Bosnian Serb forces, where he had to negotiate that on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, for that answer. Now I'd like to leave Srebrenica and talk a little bit more about the situation in Sarajevo during your tenure as Chief of Staff for the UNPROFOR BH command. In your 92 ter statement which is before us, at paragraph 11 of the same which is on page 3 in both languages, you -- I'll wait for it to get there. You talk about the Bosnian Muslim side in Sarajevo using mobile mortars to provoke a retaliation from the Serb side. Now, I do understand that you personally did not witness the actual mortars in question, and I'd like for you to explain for us the bases for your conclusion that the BiH Muslims were using vehicles, civilian vehicles, to launch from around the city with these mobile mortars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I see that the statement does reflect that mortars were mounted on a vehicle with an open roof. I don't know that there is a specific reference to civilian vehicles. I assume that's the case but I don't know that that's the case based on the statement, and I don't know if Mr. Ivetic does. But to the extent that that informs the answer I would expect Mr. Ivetic perhaps might frame it more accurately.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could perhaps assist. The 2006 statement prepared by the Office of the Prosecutor signed by this witness in paragraph 18 refers to a civilian car, and I was trying to avoid having to go through that whole statement with the witness to see if he recalled that indication. I make an offer of proof that it's in there and if counsel believes it's otherwise, I could actually read the statement into the record and that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I accept that. That's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, therefore the whole debate was unnecessary. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you tell us the bases for your knowledge because again I do understand that you did not eye-witness the actual mortar itself but I believe you do have personal knowledge that led you to believe that the BiH side was using open-roofed civilian cars to fire mobile mortars around Sarajevo. Could you tell us what that personal knowledge that you have is?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to start, my knowledge about this stems from reports of UNMOs who actually saw the vehicle with the open roof. And from my own perception, that is limited in this respect to a single incident when very close to our headquarters, behind the building where I had my bedroom, mortars were fired - and you do hear if this is close to your window - and when I approached the window to look out I saw a civilian car driving off. However, this took place in the dark so I couldn't see whether this was the actual vehicle with the open roof. However, that did make it very likely that it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. That's precisely what I understood from reading your prior -- other documentation to have been the case. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the Chamber of course is not aware of what is elsewhere because if it's not in evidence you made the singular plural, civilian cars. Is that also to be found there? And do the parties agree on that? Then it's fine. Otherwise I would like to bring to your attention that at least the statement of the witness which is in evidence does not give any reason to use the plural.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honours. And I believe the witness has confirmed that the singular incident he knows of was one car but he had reports from UNMOs of other such incidents which would therefore make it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So other such incidents could be this one car still.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Agreed. Agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now am I correct that this mobile mortar or a mortar fired in such a manner would leave a plume of smoke which would allow the other side, that is the Bosnian Serbs, to quickly locate the origin of fire and shoot back upon it in self-defence?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that was actually the major problem because those mortars were usually fired from positions in the direct vicinity or environment of UNPROFOR facilities, either the headquarters or the barracks or the headquarters of UNPROFOR. And it is clear that then this can be traced back to the place from where the mortars were fired. The risk that UNPROFOR facilities are hit is very real.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any dispute about these matters? We have heard some quite evidence about mobile mortar, a mobile mortar or mobile mortars, being fired from within the city with the risk of return fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Indeed we have, Mr. President. I'll leave that to your discretion. It's not a matter of dispute in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But of course I would like to know whether it's a matter in dispute and that's not within our discretion. If you say you well have understood the record until now then we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we can move on [overlapping speakers] ... record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I tried to convince you that it's -- there is no reason to present repetitious evidence, no reason to present evidence on matters which are not in dispute, but it seems that you have difficulties in understanding it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I want to ask you something relative to the UNPROFOR monitoring that was underway in Sarajevo at the time. And at paragraph 13 of your statement, the 92 ter statement which is on the screen, at page 4 in both languages you talk about the radar detection equipment that you describe as being not completely accurate in the early days. And I want to make it clear, for the record, that this inaccurate radar detection equipment you're talking about is the so-called Cymbeline system.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. That was what I saw as a somewhat outdated mortar-tracking radar system that the French used and which naturally allowed you to conclude that mortars were being fired. But the exact source of those grenades, for the identification of that exact source, they were not very accurate, contrary to, in fact, the equipment that was implemented on Mount Igman in the course of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, was there any dispute about this? We have heard quite a bit of evidence in detail about these matters. Cymbeline system inaccuracy, any dispute?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It's a charged incidents in the indictment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking -- I mean, that's not an answer to my question. My question was whether there is any dispute about this, about the system being the Cymbeline system and it being inaccurate, to some extent. We have heard detailed evidence about that. Should we hear from every witness the same evidence because it's part of the indictment, Mr. Ivetic? That is what you suggest apparently.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's not what I suggest, Your Honours. We have had a charged indictment where the sole evidence for it is -- the major evidence for it based upon the reliability of the Cymbeline system. And we have a witness who has very specific direct individual knowledge about it that I'm trying to elicit because its towards a direct charge in the indictment that is being charged against my client, which I believe in every court of law you are entitled to present evidence contrary to a charged indictment event, Your Honours. Please correct me if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not if it is repetitious, if it's not challenged.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then, Your Honours, are they dropping that from the indictment? Is the Prosecution willing to drop that from the indictment? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. Your questions are about facts, Mr. Ivetic. If you question a witness, you do not ask a witness: Is the charge in the indictment accurate or not? You're asking him about facts. And those facts have been dealt with in detail before this Court and seems in respect of the matters you're raising in your questions, seems to be not in dispute and repetitious, and that's the reason why I intervened. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, if you want to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There's just a couple of things, Mr. President. Paragraph 13 is what Mr. Ivetic was referring to in the statement. The witness states that the mortar detection equipment was not completely accurate, and at paragraph 14, in the last line of that paragraph, he specifically refers to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Cymbeline.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- the Cymbeline system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That of course, Mr. Vanderpuye, there was no need to repeat what I already brought to the attention of Mr. Ivetic. Cymbeline was mentioned by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we are not going to enter into a debate. This is not a debating club. This is a court of law. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is, Your Honours. And for the record, so that the record is abundantly clear, this paragraph also talks about another radar system. The witness has mentioned another radar system, so I'm perfectly entitled to try to determine whether Cymbeline is the one that is inaccurate or it is the other system that he's talked about and to get that information so we have a full picture of what happened in August of 1995 when General Smith decided to call for air strikes against the Serbs, which is a critical point to the reliability of General Smith and all his evidence that has been presented by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Put a focused question on that saying: You're talking about the Cymbeline system, you're talking about another system, was that other system or was it only the Cymbeline system which was inaccurate or were both inaccurate. Then you have a clear, focused question which meets all the needs of the Defence and gives clear answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And which would have been a compound question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. -- I said no debating club. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct, sir, that with respect to the Cymbeline system it had to be switched on after you first hear the firing start and that you had to manually move around the radar to have that system function?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of this. I know that the French used it. I don't have specific knowledge of how the system worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is your -- is the system that you talked about on Mount Igman, am I correct that that was specifically aimed at the Bosnian Serb positions to track for purposes of the rapid reaction force located thereupon to track any potential mortar rounds coming from Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the radar covered the entire area but I don't know in detail. I think at any rate that the radar covered the air space over Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And to be clear now if we can dilate upon the incident known as the Markale II shelling which occurred in late August of 1995 and the final report prepared by BH command, authorised by General Rupert Smith, your superior, that conclusively determined that the shells must have come from the Serb side were relying upon this Cymbeline radar detection system which you have identified as being inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRICK NICOLAI [Resumed]
